analysis.one_liner: Requires big political spenders to name their donors and bans election spending by government contractors and foreign-controlled firms.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a floor vote: Senate Republicans twice blocked it from debate, 57-41 in July and 59-39 in September 2010, one vote short of the 60 needed to proceed.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision allowed corporations and unions to spend unlimited treasury money on elections, this bill would have required anyone spending $10,000 or more on political ads to disclose their top funders within 24 hours. It would also have barred companies with federal contracts worth $10 million or more, firms that took TARP bailout money, and foreign-controlled corporations from spending on federal elections. The bill never came up for an up-or-down vote because Senate Republicans twice blocked the motion to begin debate.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would have been able to see within a day who was paying for the political ads they watch, and shareholders and members of organizations spending on elections, who would have learned how their money was used.

how_it_helps.text: Anyone making independent expenditures of $10,000 or more would have had to file an electronic report within 24 hours, with the information posted publicly on the FEC website in searchable, downloadable form.

Corporations, unions, and tax-exempt groups spending on elections would have had to identify their major funders in their reports, and broadcast ads would have carried spoken statements naming who was behind them.

Companies holding federal contracts worth $10 million or more and firms that received TARP bailout assistance would have been barred from making independent expenditures or electioneering communications, addressing the risk that campaign spending shapes contract awards.
The existing ban on campaign spending by foreign nationals would have been extended to foreign-controlled domestic corporations, with the CEO required to certify compliance before spending.
Registered lobbyists would have had to report their clients' independent expenditures and electioneering communications, letting the public examine links between that spending and official actions.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, and tax-exempt political groups that spend on federal elections would have lost the ability to keep their funders anonymous, and government contractors, TARP recipients, and foreign-controlled firms would have lost the ability to spend at all.

drawbacks.text: The bill created an exemption from donor disclosure for tax-exempt groups with at least 500,000 dues-paying members in every state and minimal corporate funding, which advantages long-established large organizations over newer or smaller advocacy groups.

It extended the window during which electioneering communications must be reported and disclaimed from 60 to 120 days before a general election, which reaches further into the period when issue groups discuss public policy.

Donor disclosure imposes reporting and compliance costs on advocacy organizations of all kinds; the bill itself added protections against threats and harassment of disclosed donors, an acknowledgment of that concern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is transparency: voters learn who is paying for campaign ads within a day, in exchange for reporting burdens on the groups doing the spending. The design has a real flaw in the large-membership carve-out, which let some of the biggest, oldest organizations keep their funders private while requiring newer and smaller groups to disclose. The contractor and foreign-money bans are narrower but address straightforward conflicts of interest. On balance the bill would have made the post-Citizens United spending landscape substantially more visible to voters, at a modest cost in compliance and some asymmetric burdens.

outcome.mechanism: The bill needed 60 senators to agree to cut off debate before it could even reach the floor; Democrats came up one vote short on the second attempt, so the Senate never voted on the bill itself.

narrative.text: Senator Schumer introduced the bill on July 21, 2010, as a response to the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision, which had struck down limits on corporate and union treasury spending in elections.
On July 27, 2010, a first attempt to cut off debate on the motion to proceed failed 57-41, with 56 Democrats and one independent in favor and all 40 voting Republicans plus one Democrat opposed.

Majority Leader Reid brought the bill back on September 23, 2010, and the second vote to cut off debate failed 59-39, with every Democrat and both independents present in favor and all 39 voting Republicans opposed.
Falling one vote short of the 60 needed, the bill never received an up-or-down vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations, unions, and tax-exempt groups that spent or planned to spend on the 2010 elections without naming their funders, along with government contractors and foreign-controlled firms, kept the status quo because nothing replaced the bill.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its consideration.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Moved to proceed to the bill, filed cloture motions, and brought it back for a second attempt after the first failed.

for.name: 57 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously present to cut off debate and advance the bill on the second vote.

for.name: 1 Independent and 1 Independent-Democrat Senator
for.what_they_did: Voted to cut off debate on both cloture attempts.

against.name: 39 of 40 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted as a bloc against both attempts to cut off debate, keeping the bill from reaching the floor; no Republican ever voted for it.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, which would have required disclosure of corporate-funded election spending.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's disclosure requirements even after receiving a large-membership exemption in the House version.

sides.party_line_note: The fight was almost perfectly partisan: on the second cloture vote all 57 Democrats and both independents present voted to proceed and all 39 voting Republicans opposed; on the first vote, one Democrat joined 40 Republicans in opposition, 57-41.

industries.note: Citizens United let corporations spend unlimited treasury money on elections through vehicles that kept funders hidden; the bill would have required disclosure of the largest funders within 24 hours. Voters would have been able to weigh the ads knowing who paid for them.

Companies with federal contracts of $10 million or more would have been barred from independent expenditures and electioneering communications, closing a channel where campaign spending can influence contract awards.
Firms that received bailout funds would have been barred from campaign contributions and election spending until the assistance was repaid.
The ban on foreign-national election spending would have been extended to U.S. corporations with significant foreign ownership or control, with a CEO certification required before spending.

Unions would have been covered by the same donor-disclosure rules as corporations, but the bill preserved their ability to spend and the large-membership exemption in the disclosure rules favored big, long-established membership organizations.

These groups, the main post-Citizens United vehicles for undisclosed spending, would have had to name their major funders, but organizations with 500,000 or more dues-paying members and little corporate money were exempted.
